newsitem.title: USA: Clinton puts political spin on human rights speech.
newsitem.headline: Clinton puts political spin on human rights speech.

text.p: Giving International Human Rights Day a domestic political twist, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday urged the Republican Senate to ratify a U.N. agreement to ban all forms of discrimination against women.

Democrat Clinton, re-elected last month with strong support from women voters, also committed the United States to provide up to $4 million for programmes designed to fight the exploitation and abuse of women in Africa, Asia and elsewhere.

"If women are free from violence, if they are healthy and educated, if they can live and work as full and equal partners in any society, their families will flourish, and when they do, communities and nations will thrive," he said.

The president spoke at a White House ceremony after he and his wife Hillary, an outspoken champion of women's rights, met privately with six prominent women human rights activists from the United States, Sudan and Kenya.
He said people everywhere must strive to eliminate domestic violence, use of rape as a weapon of war, sweatshop work conditions and other practices that victimise women.

The Human Rights Day ceremony came one day after Clinton met Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian despite complaints from human rights advocates that Chi helped crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Clinton, who has defended high-level contacts with Chinese officials as essential to peace and stability in Asia, made no mention of the complaints about his talks with Chi. Nor did he single out any nation for criticism on human rights.
Chi was chief of the general staff during the June 4, 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.

A U.S. human rights group, Human Rights Watch, last week accused the Clinton administration and other major powers of putting profits ahead of human rights, weakening efforts to stop offences around the world.

Other critics have zeroed in on contributions to Clinton's Democratic party by wealthy Indonesians, suggesting this may have led the administration to soften criticism of Indonesia's hard line against East Timor independence activists.
Clinton chose to ignore such criticism, but did rebuke the Republican-led Senate for its inaction on a United Nations convention banning discrimination against women.

"Many, many many other nations have done this. And in our country, where we have worked so hard against domestic violence and for the empowerment (of women), it is, to say the least, an embarrassment that the United States has not done this, and there is no excuse for this to continue," he said.

The $4 million that he committed for women's rights will be spent on such projects as aiding women refugees in Rwanda, victims of violence and discrimination in Africa and Asia and the prevention of child prostitution in Thailand.
